headline: Cooper Investors initiated a position in Aurizon after a 15%-plus share price drop, citing trough earnings, infrastructure-like asset undervaluation, and multiple growth catalysts
reasoning: Aurizon, Australia's largest railroad business, fell more than 15% after its first-half result due to weather-related volume shortfalls in coal haulage, which Cooper Investors views as a temporary impact on profitability. The stock was purchased at approximately 12-13x PE, which the firm considers cheap for an infrastructure-like business, noting that comparable regulated asset Dalrymple Bay Coal Terminal trades at over 1.3x asset base, implying the market ascribes very little value to Aurizon's non-network businesses. Cooper Investors identifies FY23 as the trough earnings year, with growth catalysts including volume recovery, India-driven met coal demand, CPI-linked contracts above cost inflation, efficiency savings via outsourcing and 'trainguard' technology, a significant WACC reset for regulated track revenue, and new bulk contract wins. US railroad peers have achieved 15-20% EPS growth p.a. from just 1-2% volume growth via pricing and mix benefits, and Aurizon's management team and board are rated highly by the firm. The growing Bulk business (hauling grain, rare earths, iron ore, copper, nickel and containerised freight) further diversifies the revenue mix away from coal over time.
quote: After its first half result (presented in February), Aurizon's shares fell by more than 15% when the company delivered a lower than expected profit result, as poor weather (rain) resulted in reduced coal volumes. However, this impact on profit is temporary with volumes expected to fully recover going forward. The Fund bought its position shortly after the result. At that point Aurizon was trading on a 12-13x PE ratio. At a headline level, this is a low rating given Aurizon is an infrastructure-like business... If we were to apply this 1.3x multiple to Aurizon, then the market is ascribing very little value to the rest of Aurizon's business. Regardless of how we value the stock, Aurizon appears 'cheap' relative to comparable infrastructure assets and offshore listed railroad peers. On closer inspection post its half year result, it was clear to us that FY23 will be the trough year for earnings for Aurizon and there are a number of reasons why earnings should grow solidly in coming years.
episode_title: CI Brunswick Fund Quarterly Report 30 June 2023

headline: Cooper Investors views Aurizon as offering near-term earnings growth from regulated returns and normalising coal volumes, with bulk providing a longer-term hedge as energy transition proceeds
reasoning: Coal represents 86% of Aurizon's 1H23 earnings and offers material near-term growth: the regulated return building blocks for FY24-27 are largely known, and coal haulage volumes have been suppressed by above-average rainfall over three years and are expected to recover with the onset of an El Niño event. Longer term, coal will be a headwind but Australian coal is expected to gain market share given its higher quality and lower production cost. Investment in bulk provides partial mitigation, as bulk contracts are above the cost of capital and trains can be repurposed. Bulk is also a partial hedge against coal decline given the critical minerals volumes required for global net zero.
quote: Coal was 86% of Aurizon's earnings in 1H23 and offers material near-term growth given: i) the building blocks for the regulated return on the below rail business for the period FY24-27 are largely known; and ii) coal haulage volumes have been impacted by above average rainfall over the past three years, which is expected to improve with the commencement of an El Niño event (as predicted by the Bureau of Meteorology). Coal will be a headwind in the medium to long-term as the world transitions to clean energy, but Australian coal is expected to take market share given it is higher quality (less emissions) with a lower cost-to-produce. Aurizon's investment in bulk should also partly mitigate the impact. Bulk contract returns are expected to be lower than thermal or met coal contracts but are still above the company's cost of capital (particularly where trains can be repurposed). We also see bulk as a partial hedge for coal as the energy transition proceeds given the quantum of critical minerals that will be required to meet global net zero objectives.
episode_title: CI Australian Equities Fund Quarterly Report 30 June 2023

headline: Cooper Investors exits Aurizon position as volume growth opportunities are limited and low interest rate environment threatens regulatory reset of network returns
reasoning: Cooper Investors had held AZJ as a core position for much of its listed history, re-establishing the position in late 2018 on confidence that management would secure a favourable commercial agreement with miners, extract balance sheet latency and deliver further cost-outs. The turnaround in the bulk business far exceeded expectations, but it is a small contributor to the group. quote: We also exited our position in Aurizon (AZJ). We have followed AZJ closely since its IPO and it has been one of the portfolio's core positions for a large part of this period. We re-established a position in AZJ towards the back end of 2018 as we had confidence management would reach a commercial agreement with the miners that would yield a higher return on the network asset, there was latency in the balance sheet, and further cost-out opportunities. We regard both the board and management team very highly, which is reflected in a well-executed strategy in a challenging environment. The turnaround in the bulk business has far exceeded our expectations, but it is a small contributor to the group. Outside of the further efficiency benefits in the above rail coal haulage business, we think the opportunities to grow volume are more limited in the current environment. If the current low interest rate environment persists, the return on the network asset will be reset at a much lower rate in the next regulatory period starting in July 2023, although there will be some offset from lower interest costs. On balance, we decided to sell our position and re-allocate the capital into other areas of the portfolio which hold more opportunity.

headline: Airlie adds to Aurizon after admitting entry-price mistake, attracted by ~9% grossed-up dividend yield and potential upside from coal ban lift
reasoning: Airlie invested in Aurizon at $5 but the share price fell to around $3.80 as the Chinese coal ban hit coal pricing and sentiment. Although Aurizon's earnings are not directly linked to the coal price, half its business is railing coal to port and volumes have suffered from the blacklisting. Airlie acknowledges their entry price failed to account for growing risks of collateral damage in a trade war with China. They have added to the position at the current price, which offers a grossed-up dividend yield of close to 9%, with share price upside if and when the coal ban is lifted.
quote: These include investing in Aurizon at $5, with the share price falling over the year to around $3.80, as the Chinese coal ban hit coal pricing and sentiment. While Aurizon's earnings aren't directly linked to the coal price, half its business is railing coal to port, and this business has seen volumes suffer due to the blacklisting. We have added to our position at the current share price, which offers a grossed up dividend yield of close to 9%, with share price upside if/when the coal ban is lifted. Clearly in hindsight our entry price failed to account for the growing risks of collateral damage in a trade war with China.
